column1: # The ideas the pages explain simply (lesson::eli5): id, the term, the explanation, then optionally a worked example and the slug of the lesson that teaches it. Tab-separated. A page links a word to its id; the reader opens it.

column3: A language model is a program that continues text: you give it some words and it works out what could come next. Nobody wrote its rules by hand; it was shaped by being shown a huge amount of text. What it learned is stored as numbers.

A weight is one of the numbers inside a model. Picture a mixing desk with billions of little knobs: each knob is a weight, and how they are all set decides what the model does. Learning means turning the knobs.
A table is numbers set out in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet with nothing but numbers in it. Mathematicians call it a matrix. "4 x 4" means 4 rows and 4 columns, so 16 numbers.

A model works in steps, like stations on an assembly line. Each station takes a list of numbers, mixes them using its own table of weights, and hands a new list to the next station. One station is a layer.

column2: multiplying a table by a list
column3: Take one row of the table. Multiply each of its numbers by the matching number of the list, and add the results: that gives one number. Do the same for every row and you have a new list, one number for each row. In the lessons it is written as two names side by side, the table first and then the list.
column4: Take the table with rows (1, 2) and (3, 4), and the list (10, 1). Row 1 gives 1 × 10 + 2 × 1 = 12. Row 2 gives 3 × 10 + 4 × 1 = 34. The new list is (12, 34).

column3: A model that already knows a lot is given extra lessons on one particular thing, the way a trained cook learns a new cuisine. The lessons work by nudging its weights. It is adjusting, not starting over.

Training is practice with correction. The model answers, the answer is compared with the one wanted, and the weights are nudged a little so the next answer is closer. Then again, many thousands of times.

For each weight, the gradient says which way to turn that knob, and how hard, to make the answer a little less wrong. Like feeling which way the ground slopes under your feet when you want to walk downhill.

The usual training method does not trust one nudge alone. For each weight it remembers the recent nudges, and how large they were, and moves by that memory. That is two more remembered numbers for every weight being trained.
Write over a page of your notebook and the old notes are gone. What a model knows is in its weights, so changing all of them to learn one new thing can write over what it knew, sometimes badly.
Frozen weights are knobs with tape over them: training is not allowed to turn them. They still do their work every time the model runs. They just never change.

An adapter is a small add-on beside a layer, like a clip-on lens on a camera. The camera is not altered; the lens changes the picture. Only the adapter has numbers that are trained, and it can be taken off again.

LoRA is one way to build an adapter: two thin tables, one that squeezes the input of the layer down to a few numbers, and one that spreads those few back out. What comes out is added to what the layer gives anyway. The name is short for low-rank adaptation.

Rank is how narrow the middle of the adapter is: how many numbers the input is squeezed into before being spread out again. Rank 1 is a single number, like summing up a whole room on one dial. A higher rank lets more through, and needs more numbers.
column4: A layer takes a list of 4 numbers. At rank 1 the adapter first boils those 4 down to 1 number, then spreads that 1 back out to 4. At rank 2 it boils them down to 2 numbers, so more of the input gets through, and it has twice as many numbers of its own.

column3: The number the strength s is set from, chosen before training: a volume knob for the adapter. At 0 the adapter adds nothing and the layer behaves as it did before. Turn it up and whatever the adapter adds counts for more.
column4: If the adapter would add (7, 0, -7, 3.5) at a strength of 2, then at a strength of 1 it adds half of that, and at 0 it adds nothing.

column3: Once training is over, what the adapter adds can be added into a copy of the table of the layer, giving one ordinary table that does the same job, so nothing extra is computed when the model runs. It is a choice, not a must: the original table is still there, and an adapter kept apart can be taken off or swapped for another.

The cost of training goes with how many numbers are being trained. A table with 4096 rows and 4096 columns holds 4096 x 4096 numbers. The two thin tables of an adapter hold only rank x (rows + columns).
column4: A table of 4 rows and 4 columns holds 4 × 4 = 16 numbers. An adapter of rank 1 for it holds 1 × (4 + 4) = 8.

column3: X_eTaL is the small programming language the computations on this page are written in. It is an array language: one short instruction works on a whole list or table of numbers at once, so the code stays close to the mathematics. You do not need to know it: every piece shown here is explained.

X_eTaL reads a line from the right: each word takes everything to its right as its input. So in "B times A times x" the rightmost pair, A times x, is worked out first, and B is then applied to that result.
A function is a named recipe: hand it ingredients and it hands back a result. X_eTaL draws the name of a function with one letter underlined. The signs + and x (times) are functions too.

A library is a box of ready-made, tested functions, like a toolbox. The line that reads "lo:" use< "LoRA" opens the toolbox called LoRA and gives it the short name lo. After that, a name drawn with a small raised lo in front of it means: that tool, from that toolbox.

Several things inside round brackets, with commas between, are handed over together as one bundle. (W, A, B, s) is the layer and its adapter in one bundle: the frozen table, the two thin tables and the strength.

In the code, "multiply a table by a list" is written with three words: a quoted +, a quoted x (times), and inner. Together they say: pair the numbers up, multiply each pair, add the results. The quote mark before + and x hands those two operations over to inner instead of doing them right away.

To find the rank of a table, count how many of its rows say something new, that is, are not just a multiple or a mix of rows already counted. Gram-Schmidt is the standard step-by-step way of doing that count.
Computers keep decimals with tiny rounding errors. "Within 1e-12" means two results agree to 12 decimal places: the same for every practical purpose.
Models are sized by how many weights (also called parameters) they have. Seven billion is a common size for a model that runs on a good laptop or one graphics card.
In the code, the arrow ← gives a value a name: the name is on its left, the value on its right. So "x ← 1 2 3 4" reads: x is the list 1, 2, 3, 4. (It is typed as a colon and an equals sign.)
A line that starts with the sign ⍝ is a note for the reader, not an instruction: the computer skips it. In this program the notes say in words what the lines under them do.
When the program asks a yes-or-no question, such as "are these two results the same?", it prints 1 for yes and 0 for no.

The number the correction is multiplied by before it is added. LoRA sets it to alpha divided by the rank, so that the correction stays about the same size when the rank is changed; lesson 4 shows a second rule for it. In LoRA hello the rank is 1, so there s is alpha itself.
What the adapter adds to the output of the layer. The frozen layer gives its usual answer; the correction is the small list of numbers added on top. Other texts call it the update, or delta.

A list is some numbers in a row, in a fixed order: (1, 2, 3, 4) is a list of four numbers. The lessons give a list a short name, often a single letter such as x, so they can talk about all of its numbers at once.
A stage is one step of a calculation: it takes the numbers worked out so far, does one thing to them, and hands on new numbers. A calculation in four stages is four such steps, one after another.
One input together with the output wanted for it. Training is done on a set of examples: the model's output for each input is compared with the one wanted.
column4: On this page an example is a list of 8 numbers going in and the list of 8 wanted out, made by a layer the adapter never sees.

column3: One number that says how wrong the model is on a set of examples: the differences between its outputs and the ones wanted, squared (so that a miss either way counts, and a large miss counts much more), added up, and halved. Training tries to make it smaller. Zero would mean every output exactly right.
column4: Outputs (1, 2) wanted (1, 4): the differences are 0 and -2, their squares 0 and 4, the sum 4, the loss 2.

column3: Examples kept back from training and used only to measure. The loss on them says whether what was learned carries over to inputs the model has not practiced on, which is the kind it will meet afterward.

How far the weights move on each step of training, as a fraction of what the gradient asks for. Too small and training crawls; too large and each step overshoots, so the loss jumps about instead of falling.

The usual way of taking training steps. Instead of moving by the latest gradient alone, it keeps running averages of the recent gradients and of their sizes for every weight trained, and moves by those, so one unusual step does not throw it off.

When a model fits the examples it trained on more and more closely while getting no better, or worse, on examples it has not seen: it has learned those particular examples rather than what they have in common. Too few examples for the size of what is being trained invites it.

What was written down during training, every so many steps: the loss, and the weights being trained as they were then. A page that has the record can show any point of the training again without training again.

LoRA-FA is LoRA with the first small table, A, frozen: made once from a seed and not trained; only B moves. That halves the numbers to train and the optimizer's memory, and a saved adapter need not store A, since the seed regrows it. The price: every row of the update s B A is a mix of A's rows, so the update can only lie where those rows let it. (Zhang and others, 2023.)

Full fine-tuning moves every number of the layer (or of the whole model) during training, with no adapter: the table W itself changes. Nothing limits what it can reach. Its costs: a gradient for every number, two more numbers of optimizer memory for each, and a whole changed copy of the model to store afterward. Adapters trade some of that reach for smaller costs.
column4: On this page's 8 by 8 layer it trains all 64 numbers, and Adam holds 128 more.

column3: A table can be split into rank-1 pieces, largest first; its singular values are the sizes of those pieces. A table of rank 4 has four that are not 0, then zeros. The closest any table of rank k can come to it leaves out the pieces past the k-th, so the lowest loss possible at rank k is half the sum of the squared singular values after the k-th (Eckart and Young, 1936).
column4: A table with singular values 3, 2, 1 and then zeros: at rank 2 the lowest loss possible is half of 1 squared, 0.5; at rank 3 and up it is 0.

column3: Take a few lists of numbers of the same length, the rows of a table say, and all the lists you can make from them by scaling each and adding them up. That collection is a subspace: a flat region, through the origin, inside the space of all lists of that length. Two lists of 8 that do not line up give a flat sheet inside 8-dimensional space. A table's rows make its row space.

A basis of a subspace is a set of lists that span it with none to spare: every point of the subspace is one mix of them, and no list in the set is a mix of the others. The rows of the frozen A are a basis of its row space (when they are independent): each row of the update s B A is a mix of them, with B's numbers as the amounts.

The projection of a list onto a subspace is the point of the subspace nearest to it: drop a perpendicular from the list to the flat region, and the foot of it is the projection. What is left, the list minus its projection, is the remainder; its size says how much of the list lies outside the subspace. A list already in the subspace is its own projection, with a remainder of 0.
column4: On this page each learned update's rows are projected onto the frozen A's row space: LoRA-FA's remainder is 0 to rounding; LoRA's is not, at a rank under 8 (at rank 8 the row space is the whole space).

column3: Retention is what a model keeps of what it did before it learned something new. Here it is a loss: some old inputs are kept, with the outputs the layer gave them before any training, and after training the layer's loss on those old examples says how far it moved from what it did. 0 means nothing changed for them; the larger, the less was kept. It is the measure behind catastrophic forgetting.
